title: Automate contract reviews
description: A system that checks a new contract against your playbook, clause by clause, and flags every deviation by risk before anyone reads it.

pull.title: Pull
pull.content: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your computer so your local copy is up to date. Claude pulls before starting work to make sure it's building on the newest version, not an old one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

plugin.title: Plugin
plugin.content: A bundle that adds new skills, tool connectors, slash commands, or hooks to Claude Code in one install. Drop in a plugin for your team's tools and everyone on the team gets the same capabilities.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

anthropic.title: Anthropic
anthropic.content: The company that created Claude. An AI safety company focused on building reliable, interpretable AI systems.

repository.title: Repository (Repo)
repository.content: A project folder tracked by Git. Your GitHub repo is where Claude stores your code and files. When Claude 'pushes to GitHub,' it's sending changes from your computer to the online repo.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: 91% of in-house legal professionals report efficiency gains from generative AI, and 71% see an opportunity to insource contract work that used to go to outside counsel, per the [ACC and Everlaw 2025 survey](https://www.everlaw.com/press/release/acc-report-2025) of corporate law departments. It's high-volume, pattern-based, and every organization already has a playbook, even if it only lives in one person's head.

This system runs a new or counterparty-marked-up agreement against your own negotiating playbook, rating every deviation green, yellow, or red against your own risk definitions and [pulling](#tooltip-pull) fallback language straight from the playbook. [Anthropic](#tooltip-anthropic)'s Claude Legal [plugin](#tooltip-plugin) ships a dedicated `/review-contract` command for this exact pattern, and Claude Opus 4.7 scored 90.9% on Harvey's BigLaw Bench, the highest of any Claude model, per Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg.

Run it as a one-off paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt), a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill) for a recurring type, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) watching your [repository](#tooltip-repository) for new drafts. A person decides what goes back to the counterparty.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document naming where your playbook lives, which contract type it covers first, your risk categories, and who can approve a yellow flag.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that reviews contracts against our company's own playbook and flags where a document deviates from our standard positions. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what our playbook actually covers, which contract types this applies to first, how I want deviations rated by risk, what fallback language exists for each clause type, and who needs to sign off before anything goes back to a counterparty. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming your playbook, contract type, and sign-off chain keeps the review honest to your own standards instead of a generic risk scale.

items: Where your playbook lives, in a form the system can read.
Which contract types get this treatment first.
Who has authority to approve a yellow-flagged deviation without a full attorney review.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are your contract repository or CLM (Ironclad, DocuSign CLM), your document management system (iManage, NetDocuments), and e-signature (DocuSign). The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build your system and test it on a real contract, with your playbook attached. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document gives a version for your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Compare [the attached contract] against our standard playbook and flag every clause that deviates, rated by risk, with suggested fallback language.

Context: Our playbook positions are documented in [location]. This is a [contract type, e.g. MSA/NDA/vendor agreement] for [counterparty/deal context]. Prior redlines on similar deals are in [location] for reference.

Rules:
- Compare every clause against the playbook position, not just the clauses that look unusual on a skim.
- Rate each deviation green (standard), yellow (negotiable, flag for review), or red (must escalate to counsel) using our own risk definitions, not a generic legal risk scale.
- Quote the actual contract language and the actual playbook language side by side for every flag.
- Never suggest fallback language that isn't already approved in the playbook.
- Output as a clause-by-clause table with clause name, flag color, what deviates, and suggested fallback.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: rating against your own green, yellow, and red definitions keeps deviations comparable across reviewers, instead of a generic risk scale that shifts with whoever's reading.

children.text: **Review.** Check it against your scope. Every clause covered, colors matching your risk definitions, fallback pulled from the playbook?
**Feedback.** Tell it what went wrong, like a green flag that should have been yellow, and fold the correction into the risk definitions so it applies beyond this contract.

items: Schedule it. Connect your repository through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) and run this against every new draft.
Build a clause library tagged by type and past outcomes so fallback suggestions sharpen over time.
Track which flagged deviations get pushed back on versus accepted, to tighten the playbook.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) instead of a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each contract review, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, contract type, deviations flagged, flags a reviewer overturned, and playbook sections that needed updating. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the overturned-flags column shows where the comparison drifts from what reviewers decide.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few reviews straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. A playbook comparison is as good as the playbook. If positions go stale, the system confidently flags the wrong standard, so review it as often as the contracts it checks.
